passage:
Sunday night. Application number 26 went out today. Eleven rejections, fourteen silences. Santosh got his offer yesterday and threw a small party for the flat, and I cheered, then went to my room and felt hollow.
I could stop. Some nights I think about it. But I looked at the list again: three are still pending, and one rejection had a note: "Strong portfolio, not a match this round." That is not nothing.
I can't tell whether any of this will work. I'm not going to wait for luck to write to me. Tomorrow morning I'll tighten the cover letter for the design firm and send it by ten.
— Ujjwal

qa.q: How many rejections had Ujjwal received?
qa.a: Ujjwal had received eleven rejections.

qa.q: What was Ujjwal feeling after cheering for Santosh and going to the room?
qa.a: Ujjwal felt hollow and discouraged, and tempted to stop applying.

qa.q: What did Ujjwal decide to do about the design firm?
qa.a: Ujjwal decided to tighten the cover letter the next morning and send it by ten, acting without any guarantee.

qa.q: How might Santosh have seen Ujjwal's cheering at the party?
qa.a: Santosh probably took it as warm support and may not have noticed the hollow feeling afterwards, since Ujjwal went to a separate room.

grounding: A young adult applies for jobs knowing many will fail, yet continues; mature hope accepts uncertainty and still acts.

passage:
"Pallavi, you asked how I keep going with the internship hunt. Honestly? I'm Gopika, I'm twenty, and I've sent forty-three applications since January.
I've had thirty rejections, eleven silences and two interviews. One interview I bombed. The other said they'd 'keep me in mind,' which I think means no.
Every Sunday I sit at the library, make a cup of chai from the machine, and send three more. I don't tell myself 'this is the one.' I tell myself most won't work, and some day one might.
My roommate prays over each email. I'm not against that! But I noticed she stops applying when she's waiting for a sign. I'd rather keep sending while I wait.
Yesterday I got a third interview. I'm scared. I'm going anyway. That's the whole plan, really."

qa.q: How many applications has Gopika sent since January?
qa.a: Forty-three.

qa.q: How does Gopika feel about the third interview?
qa.a: Gopika feels scared but determined, choosing to go anyway without any guarantee.

qa.q: What small habit keeps Gopika's search going?
qa.a: Every Sunday at the library, sending three more applications, while expecting most to fail.

qa.q: How is the roommate's hope different from Gopika's?
qa.a: The roommate prays and then stops applying while waiting for a sign, while Gopika accepts uncertainty and keeps acting.

grounding: Shows a young adult who keeps applying knowing most applications will fail, accepting uncertainty and still acting.

passage:
June 3: Disha submitted her application for a teaching fellowship in rural Maharashtra. Twelve hundred people applied for sixty places. She told her friend Maria on the phone, "I probably won't get it. I'm applying anyway, and to three others."
June 20: The first rejection came from the Pune programme. Disha felt the sting all evening. Maria texted, "Still going?" Disha replied, "Still going," and sent off the fourth application that night.
July 15: A call for the final interview in Nashik. Disha had no idea if she'd get it. She ironed her kurta, packed her lesson plan, and got on the early bus with a knot in her stomach. On the way she drafted a fifth application, just in case.

qa.q: How many people applied for the sixty places?
qa.a: Twelve hundred people.

qa.q: What was Disha feeling on June 20?
qa.a: She felt the sting of rejection all evening but stayed determined, replying 'Still going'.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Applying to several programmes and drafting another even before the interview worked, because it kept her acting while accepting she might not get any one of them.

qa.q: How might Maria see Disha's approach?
qa.a: Maria seems supportive and a little admiring, checking in with 'Still going?' after the rejection.

grounding: Shows a young adult who keeps applying for postings despite knowing many will fail, accepting uncertainty and still acting.

passage:
"Nandini, you're sulking at that rejection email as if it's the last ship leaving," said Thomas uncle, laughing. "Let me tell you about 1989. I was twenty-one, trying to get on a merchant ship as a cadet. I went to the shipping offices in Kochi every Monday for eight months. Every Monday, no. Some clerks knew me by name. One gave me tea out of pity.
My friend Jacob said, 'If it's meant to be, it'll come.' He stopped going. He waited for a letter that never came.
I didn't know if I'd ever get a berth. I knew only that if I stopped going, I definitely wouldn't. On the thirty-fourth Monday, a captain needed someone that day. I was standing there.
It wasn't fate, kutty. It was being there on the day, without knowing."

qa.q: How long did Thomas uncle keep going to the shipping offices?
qa.a: Every Monday for eight months.

qa.q: What was young Thomas feeling during those months of Mondays?
qa.a: He felt uncertain but determined, not knowing if he'd ever get a berth yet refusing to stop.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Thomas uncle's story, and what made it possible?
qa.a: The thirty-fourth Monday, when a captain needed someone that day; it happened because he kept showing up without any guarantee.

qa.q: How is Jacob's hope different from Thomas's?
qa.a: Jacob waited for fate and stopped going, so his hope had no action, while Thomas kept acting despite uncertainty.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling how he kept applying for ship berths without any guarantee, unlike a friend who waited for fate.

passage: The power went out in the Siliguri hostel at 10:40 pm, and the application for the hotel management trainee post closed at midnight. Dolma's laptop showed 14%. It was her twenty-sixth application this month. Nineteen had never answered; four had said no. Her roommate Sonali held up a phone torch. "Why bother? They'll probably reject it anyway." "Probably," Dolma said, typing fast. "But definitely, if I don't send it." She cut the cover letter to two paragraphs to save battery, attached the certificate she had scanned that morning, and pressed submit at 11:52 with 3% left. Then she opened her notebook, drew a line under number twenty-six, and wrote twenty-seven: the airport lounge job, closes Monday.

qa.q: At what time did Dolma press submit?
qa.a: At 11:52, with 3% battery left.

qa.q: What does Dolma's reply "But definitely, if I don't send it" show about how she feels?
qa.a: She feels realistic and determined, accepting that rejection is likely but still hopeful enough to act.

qa.q: Which choice helped Dolma beat the power cut?
qa.a: Cutting the cover letter to two paragraphs saved battery and time, so the application still went in before midnight.

qa.q: How might Sonali see Dolma writing number twenty-seven?
qa.a: Sonali may feel puzzled or impressed, seeing Dolma keep going after so many silences instead of waiting for luck.

grounding: Shows a young adult who keeps applying for jobs despite likely rejections, acting with hope but without any guarantee.
